comparisons.peer_topic: CCAR stress test results and SCB determination
comparisons.peer_summary: Based on 2024 CCAR stress test results, the SCB is set at 3.2 percent, effective from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025, in accordance with Federal Reserve requirements for annual capital planning and supervisory stress testing.
comparisons.comparison:
Both Morgan Stanley and Bank of America disclosed their 2024 Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) determinations resulting from the Federal Reserve's supervisory stress tests, effective October 1, 2024. Morgan Stanley reported a higher SCB of 6.0% driven by a 4.6% projected CET1 decline and a dividend add-on, whereas Bank of America reported a lower SCB of 3.2% based on its CCAR results. Both firms explicitly tied these buffer calculations to Federal Reserve requirements for annual capital planning and supervisory stress testing.

Target: "On June 26, 2024, the Federal Reserve published summary results of its supervisory stress tests of each large BHC, in which the projected decline in our CET1 ratio in the severely adverse scenario increased from the prior annual supervisory stress test by 50 basis points, from 4.1% to 4.6%. ... Together with other features of the regulatory capital framework, this SCB results in an aggregate Standardized Approach Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 13.5%."
Peer: "Based on 2024 Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) stress test results, our SCB is 3.2 percent effective from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025."

comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup's CET1 Capital ratio increased to 13.6% as of December 31, 2024, from 13.4% in 2023, driven by net income and a decrease in risk-weighted assets, partially offset by dividends, share repurchases, and AOCI movements.
comparisons.comparison:
While Morgan Stanley disclosed its specific SCB calculation (13.5% aggregate CET1 ratio) derived from the 2024 stress test cycle, Citigroup disclosed its ending CET1 capital ratio performance for the same period, noting it reached 13.6%. Both figures represent the resulting capital adequacy metrics for major banks under the Basel III Standardized Approach, though Morgan Stanley focused on the regulatory buffer outcome while Citigroup focused on the performance drivers (net income, RWA changes) affecting the ratio.

Both disclosures highlight the Federal Reserve's determination of capital buffers based on supervisory stress test scenarios.
